title: Random Forest Decision Tree Visualizer
description: Set a hypothetical patient profile (age, BMI, smoking status, hypertension, physical activity) and see how one decision tree classifies it, how 20 trees trained on bootstrap samples vote, and how the majority vote becomes the forest prediction. Includes a ROC curve for the forest. Trained in the browser on synthetic data; not a clinical risk model.
creator: Introduction to Public Health Project
subject: public health
data science
machine learning
random forest
decision tree

learning_objective: Explain how a random forest turns the votes of many different decision trees into one prediction, and why the forest's answer is more stable than the answer of any single tree.
chapter_title: Data Science Advanced: Spatial Analysis and Machine Learning

educational.topic: Random forests for disease risk prediction
learningObjectives: Trace a patient's path through a decision tree
Explain bootstrap sampling and random feature selection
Explain how majority voting produces the forest prediction
Relate a vote threshold to a point on the ROC curve
prerequisites: Decision trees as yes or no questions

controls.label: Show Another Tree
controls.description: Shows the next of the 20 trees in the left panel.

controls.label: Tree icons
controls.description: Click a tree in the forest grid to show it in the left panel.

simulation.modelType: Random forest classifier trained in the browser on synthetic data

parameters.treeDepth: two levels of splits, four leaves
parameters.randomSeed: fixed, so every reader sees the same forest

assumptions: Synthetic outcome generated from an invented logistic model of age, BMI, smoking, hypertension, and inactivity
A tree votes high risk when its leaf probability is at least 50%
The forest predicts high risk when at least 10 of 20 trees vote high risk
limitations: Not a clinical risk model and not based on real patient data
Trees are much shallower and fewer than in a real random forest

pedagogical.interactionPattern: Concrete worked example that updates instantly, with no timed animation
keyQuestions: Why do trees trained on the same kind of data ask different questions?
Why is the forest's answer more stable than one tree's answer?
What changes if the vote threshold is made stricter?
commonMisconceptions: A random forest is one large decision tree
Every tree in the forest sees the same data and the same features
The 50% majority rule is the only possible threshold
assessmentOpportunities: Explain bootstrap sampling and random feature selection
State the forest prediction for a given vote count under two different thresholds
